Methods
Animals
Eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice, obtained from Beijing SiPeiFu Biotechnology Co., [SCXK (Jing) 2019–0004], were housed in groups of 4–5 under standard laboratory conditions with a 12-hour light/dark cycle and ad libitum food and water access. The experimental schemes involving animal care were approved by the Ethics Committee of China-Japan Friendship Hospital (Approval No. zryhyy61-24–02-25). The type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) mouse model was established according to a previously reported method
[14]
. Mice were subjected to a high-fat diet (HFD) consisting of 60 % fat for a four-week period prior to the induction of diabetes. Diabetes was established through five consecutive days of intraperitoneal streptozotocin (STZ) injections at a dose of 25 mg/kg per day. Control mice were fed a standard chow diet for four weeks prior to receiving daily intraperitoneal injections of an equivalent volume of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), for five consecutive days. Diabetes was diagnosed if plasma glucose levels surpassed 300 mg/dl sixteen days post the final STZ injection. Blood glucose levels were measured from tail vein samples using ACCU-CHEK glucose strips.
For the administration of adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) into the lateral ventricles (i.c.v.), mice were anesthetized via an intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital and secured in a stereotactic frame. A 0.5 μl viral preparation was delivered into each lateral ventricle using a needle connected to a 10-μl Hamilton syringe (Hamilton Medical), maintaining a flow rate of 0.25 μl per minute. The stereotactic coordinates relative to the bregma were as follows: anteroposterior −2.2 mm, mediolateral ± 1.5 mm, and dorsoventral −1.5 mm.
Novel object recognition (NOR) test and novel object location recognition (NOL) test
To evaluate cognitive processes related to learning and memory functions, the NOL and NOR tests were conducted in accordance with established protocols
[15]
, 114 days post-model establishment. Initially, mice were subjected to a 15-minute acclimation period in an empty wooden chamber. Mice were initially acclimated to a novel, empty wooden chamber for a 15-minute session. Following a 24-hour interval, animals were reintroduced to the chamber with two identical objects positioned equidistantly in opposite corners. Mice were permitted to explore freely until a cumulative exploration time of 30 s was attained for both objects. Exploration was defined as the animal's nose approaching within 2 cm of the object, excluding any instances of climbing or sitting on the object.
Twenty-four hours later, mice were reintroduced to the chamber where one familiar object had been replaced with a novel object in a different corner. Object recognition was assessed by calculating the ratio of exploration time devoted to the novel object compared to total exploration time. From each group, eight mice were randomly chosen to undergo behavioral testing. The NOL test was administered initially, followed by the NOR test four days subsequently. For the NOR test, a novel object replaced one of the familiar objects 24 h after initial exposure. The percentage of time spent exploring the novel object, relative to the total exploration time, was calculated.
Morris water maze (MWM) test
The MWM task was used to assess spatial learning and memory, as detailed in our previous study
[16]
. The experiment was performed 114 days after model establishment. The apparatus consisted of a circular pool, 150 cm in diameter, divided into four equal quadrants. The pool was filled with water (16 cm deep, 28–32 °C). A concealed escape platform was positioned at the center of a single quadrant. A submerged escape platform was positioned at the center of one quadrant of the pool. A ceiling-mounted camera connected to a computerized tracking system (DigBehv, Shanghai Jiliang Software Technology Co., China) was employed to record the swimming trajectories of the mice.
The experimental paradigm consisted of a five-day acquisition phase, during which four platform trials were administered daily, followed by a probe trial on the sixth day. Mice were introduced to the water pool during the acquisition phase, with the hidden platform positioned in a designated quadrant. Subjects were allotted 60 s to locate the platform. If unsuccessful, gentle guidance to the platform was provided, followed by a 15-second retention period to reinforce spatial memory. Performance was assessed at 90 s post-placement, with trials r conducted four times daily until no additional improvement was observed. On the sixth day, the platform was removed, allowing the mice to swim freely for 60 s from a starting point opposite the original platform location. The the time taken to locate the hidden platform (escape latency) and time spent in the target quadrant were recorded for subsequent analysis.
Hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining
To evaluate neuronal damage, HE staining was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Solarbio Science and Technology, Beijing, China). Histological alterations within the hippocampal regions were examined under an optical microscope (Olympus Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) at 400 × magnification. Neuronal quantification in the CA1, CA3, and dentate gyrus (DG) pyramidal cell layers, as well as the cortex, was conducted by counting the number of neurons within a 250-µm length in five sections per mouse. The mean neuronal count was considered the final data point.
Immunohistochemical staining
Prior to immunohistochemical (IHC) staining, tissue sections underwent deparaffinization and rehydration. Paraffin-embedded tissues were sectioned into 4–5 μm thick slices and mounted onto glass slides. IHC staining was performed using a DAB kit and an IHC kit (ZSGB-BIO, Beijing, China) according to the manufacturer's protocols with anti-4HNE antibody (cat. no. MA5-27570; 1:500 dilution; RRID: AB_2735095, Invitrogen Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China). Following the staining procedure, slides underwent dehydration and clearing processes before being mounted using a permanent mounting medium. Images were captured at a magnification of 400 × utilizing an Olympus BX53 microscope integrated with a digital camera.
TUNEL staining
Apoptosis was evaluated using the TUNEL Apoptosis Assay Kit (C1088, Beyotime, China) in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. Hippocampal sections were fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde for a duration of 30 min, followed by two consecutive 10-minute washes in 0.01 M PBS. Permeabilization was achieved through a 5-minute incubation in 0.5 % Triton-X-100/PBS at room temperature. Subsequently, sections were incubated with TUNEL assay solution for 60 min at 37 °C in the dark, protected from evaporation. Nuclear staining was performed using DAPI for 10 min, followed by three 5-minute PBS washes. Coverslips were applied using a 50 % glycerin mounting medium. Stained sections were examined under a fluorescence microscope (Olympus Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) at 200 × magnification. Five randomly selected fields were analyzed to quantify total neurons and TUNEL-positive neurons. The proportion of apoptotic neurons was determined by calculating the ratio of TUNEL-positive neurons to total neurons multiplied by 100 %.
Lactate measurement
After homogenization of frozen hippocampal tissue in 1 mL of ice-cold lactate assay buffer, the samples were centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 5 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was analyzed using an L-lactate assay (cat. no. A019-2–1, Jiancheng, Nanjing, China) to quantify lactate levels following the manufacturer's protocol. For in vitro experiments, cells were harvested by centrifugation, resuspended in pre-cooled PBS, and pelleted again. The supernatant was removed, and the cell pellet was resuspended in 1 mL of lactate assay buffer. Cell disruption was achieved through sonication in an ice bath utilizing a 200 W sonicator. The sonication was performed in 30 cycles, each consisting of a 3-second pulse and a 7-second rest, for a total sonication time of 5 min. Following the initial centrifugation, the resulting supernatant underwent a second centrifugation at 12,000 × g for 5 min at 4 °C. The clarified supernatant was then transferred to a fresh Eppendorf tube. Lactate levels were quantified in both brain tissue homogenates and microglial cell culture supernatants using a commercial lactate analyzer (Roche, Mannheim, Germany).
Quantitative proteomics analysis
Hippocampus samples from each group were measured in triplicate. The proteomic analysis was performed at the Jingjie PTM BioLab Co., Ltd. (Hangzhou, China) Proteomics Facility, following standard protocols. Proteins extracted from hippocampal cell lysates were quantified using the BCA protein assay. For digestion, proteins were subjected to trypsin treatment at a protein-to-protease ratio of 50:1 (w/w) for 12 h. Subsequently, cysteines were reduced and alkylated through sequential incubation with 5 mM dithiothreitol at 56 °C for 30 min, followed by 11 mM iodoacetamide for 15 min at room temperature in the dark. The resulting peptides were resuspended in mobile phase A (0.1 % formic acid + 2 % acetonitrile) for liquid chromatography. Separation was carried out using a NanoElute ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography system (Bruker Daltonics). The gradient for phase B (0.1 % formic acid + 100 % acetonitrile) was as follows: 6–24 % for 0–70 min, 24–35 % for 70–84 min, 35–80 % for 84–87 min, and held at 80 % from 87 to 90 min, with a flow rate of 450 nL/min. During the separation process, peptides were ionized using a capillary ion source and analyzed with a TIMS-TOF Pro mass spectrometer. The pulse voltage was set to 1.65 kV, and both peptide precursors and their secondary fragments were analyzed using high-resolution LC/Q-TOF-MS, with a secondary mass spectrometry scan range of 400 to 1500
m
/
z
.
Differential expression analysis across the three groups was performed using the DESeq2 R software package (version 3.14). Fold-changes were calculated to compare the groups, with proteins showing an adjusted p-value of less than 0.05 and an absolute fold-change greater than 1.2 being considered differentially expressed. Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses for differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were conducted using the clusterProfiler package (version 3.4.4). KEGG analysis was performed using KEGG Mapper (
https://www.genome.jp/kegg/mapper.html
).
Cell culture
Primary microglias cultures were derived from C57BL/6 mice in accordance with established protocols. The cortices of two-month-old mice were finely minced in Hibernate A medium supplemented with B27 (Gibco) and subsequently dissociated using a papain solution (Worthington). Following tissue trituration, the cells were isolated via density gradient centrifugation employing Optiprep (Sigma-Aldrich). Primary microgliass were maintained in either high- or low-glucose Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS, GibcoBRL) at 37 °C with 5 % CO2. Human monocytic cell line HMC3 (RRID: CVCL_II76) was cultured in Minimum Essential Medium (MEM) supplemented with Non-Essential Amino Acids (NEAA) and 10 % FBS. Cells were subcultured every 3 to 4 days and maintained in a temperature-controlled incubator set at 37 °C. Microglials were cultured at a density of 1 × 10
6
cells per well in a six-well plate. Cells were cultured with or without NaLa (25 μM, Sigma-Aldrich, MO, USA) and incubated for 24 h. In order to investigate the mechanisms underlying diabetes, we modeled the in vivo diabetic state using a well-established in vitro system of HG and Pal
[17]
. Cells were treated with an HG + Pal medium, consisting of 200 μM palmitate and 25 mM glucose. To assess the role of LDH, we inhibited its activity by treating cells with 50 mM oxamate for 2 h prior to subsequent experiments.
Western blot analysis
Total protein concentration in both in vitro and in vivo microglia was quantified prior to sample preparation. Subsequently, a loading buffer was added to the protein samples, which were then subjected to denaturation through high-temperature incubation. Following denaturation, protein samples were resolved by SDS-PAGE (Wako Supersep™Ace, 5–20 %) and subsequently transferred to PVDF membranes (Invitrogen) using transfer buffer. To minimize non-specific binding, membranes were blocked using a 5 % solution of non-fat blocking grade milk. Primary antibodies against Pan Kla (RRID:AB_2942013, Jingjie PTM BioLabs, Hangzhou, China), histone H3K18 (RRID:AB_3076698, Jingjie PTM BioLabs, Hangzhou, China), histone H4K12 (RRID:AB_2941896, Jingjie PTM BioLabs, Hangzhou, China), histone H4K8 (RRID: AB_3101829, Jingjie PTM BioLabs, Hangzhou, China), histone H4 (RRID: AB_3101866, Jingjie PTM BioLabs, Hangzhou, China), CBP (cat. no. 7389; RRID: AB_2616020, Cell Signaling Technology, Massachusetts, USA), P300 (cat. no. 57625; RRID: AB_3068009, Cell Signaling Technology, Massachusetts, USA), FOXO1 (cat. no. MA5-14846; RRID: AB_10987316, Invitrogen Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China) and PGC-1α (cat. no. ab191838; RRID: AB_2721267, Abcam, Cambridge, UK) were applied to the blots overnight. After incubation with TBST, protein bands were probed with a secondary antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Boston, MA, USA) for 1 h at room temperature. ECL was employed to visualize the immunoreactive bands. Densitometric analysis was conducted using ImageJ software to quantify the specific antibody fluorescence intensity of the protein bands.
Immunofuorescent staining
Following deparaffinization and rehydration, sections were subjected to antigen retrieval. Nonspecific binding was blocked by incubating sections with goat serum for 1 h at room temperature. Subsequently, sections were incubated with primary antibodies against Iba1 (cat. no. MA5-50414; 1:500 dilution; RRID: AB_3094208, Invitrogen Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China), Pan Kla (cat. no. PTM-1401RM; 1:100 dilution; RRID:AB_2942013, PTM BIO, Hangzhou, China), H4K12la (cat. no. PTM-1415RM; 1:100 dilution; RRID:AB_2941896, PTM BIO, Hangzhou, China), Aβ (cat. no. MA1-140; 1:500 dilution; RRID: AB_2536844, Invitrogen Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China), FOXO1 (cat. no. MA5-14846; 1:500 dilution; RRID: AB_10987316, Invitrogen Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China), incubated with secondary antibodies conjugated with Alexa Fluor dyes: Alexa Fluor 488 (green), Alexa Fluor 594 (red), and Alexa Fluor 750 (pink) (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China), and then mounted on slides. Immunofluorescence-stained sections were visualized and captured at high resolution with a Zeiss Axio Observer 3 fluorescence microscope. ImageJ software was utilized to measure the mean fluorescence intensity within defined regions of interest. Iba1- and Kla-positive cells were manually counted to determine cell numbers.
Human specimens
We recruited 42 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and 35 healthy controls from individuals undergoing physical examinations at Tangshan Gongren Hospital. Participants were recruited between January 2022 and May 2022. The diagnostic criteria for T2DM were based on the World Health Organization's recommendations. Clinical information was gathered from medical records. Global cognitive function was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Fasting blood samples were drawn from the cubital vein with the subject supine. Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of Tangshan Gongren Hospital.
Metabolomic analysis
Metabolomics analysis was conducted using UPLC-Q-TOF/MS. After pre-processing, the analysis was performed on an ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography system (UHPLC, 1290 Infinity LC, Agilent Technologies) coupled with a quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometer (AB Sciex TripleTOF 6600) at Shanghai Applied Protein Technology Co., Ltd. For HILIC separation, a 2.1 mm × 100 mm ACQUIY UPLC BEH column (1.7 µm, Waters, Ireland) was used. The raw mass spectrometry (MS) data were converted to MzXML format using ProteoWizard MSConvert and subsequently processed with the open-source software XCMS. For peak detection, the following parameters were applied: centWave
m
/
z
= 10 ppm, peakwidth = c(10, 60), and prefilter = c(10, 100). For peak grouping, the settings were bw = 5, mzwid = 0.025, and minfrac = 0.5. Isotope and adduct annotation were carried out using the CAMERA (Collection of Algorithms of MEtabolite pRofile Annotation) package. From the extracted ion features, only variables with more than 50 % non-zero measurement values in at least one group were retained. Metabolite identification was performed by comparing the accurate
m
/
z
values (<10 ppm) and MS/MS spectra against an in-house database established using authentic standards.
Isolation of microglia from adult mouse brains
Following euthanasia by intraperitoneal pentobarbital injection, mice subjected to transcardial perfusion using ice-cold phosphate-buffered saline. Brains were carefully extracted and placed on a chilled dissection plate. The cortex, olfactory bulbs, and cerebellum were removed, and the bilateral hippocampi were bilaterally dissected and collected. Tissue dissociation was was conducted using the Adult Brain Dissociation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, Germany), strictly adhering to the manufacturer's guidelines. Following myelin removal using cell debris removal buffers, the total cell pellet was resuspended in PBS supplemented with 0.5 % BSA to facilitate the subsequent isolation of specific cell types. Microglia were isolated by positive selection utilizing anti-CD11b-coated MicroBeads (130–093-634, Miltenyi Biotec) and a MACS multistand separator, as per the manufacturer’s protocol. For histone extraction and analysis, cells from three mice were pooled for each experimental sample. After confirmation by immunofluorescence, the sorted cells did not exhibit polarization and showed either no or very few cellular protrusions (
Fig. S1
).
CUT&Tag and sequencing
Isolated microglia were subjected to CUT&Tag analysis immediately following isolation. The CUT&Tag protocol was carried out according to the manufacturer's instructions using the Hieff NGS® G-Type In- situ DNA Binding Profiling Library Prep Kit for Illumina (12598ES12, Yeasen, Shanghai, China). Isolated microglia were bound to Concanavalin A-coated beads and subsequently resuspended in antibody buffer for incubation with primary antibodies specific for H4K12la. Following this, cells were incubated with corresponding secondary antibodies. Transposon activation and tagmentation of the samples were achieved using pA-Tn5 transposase. The resulting DNA fragments were subsequently isolated, amplified, and purified to generate sequencing libraries. High-throughput sequencing was conducted on an Illumina NovaSeq system, employing paired-end 150-base reads.
Real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR)
Total RNA was isolated from tissues or cells using a Trizol-based cell lysis buffer (Invitrogen, CA, USA). cDNA was subsequently synthesized from the extracted RNA using a PrimeScript™ RT reagent kit (cat. no. RR037A; Takara Bio, Inc., Dalian, China). Quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) was performed using SYBR-Green mix (Roche, Basel, Switzerland) to determine gene expression levels. Primer sequences utilized for qPCR are provided in
Table S1
. β-actin mRNA levels served as an endogenous control for normalization of gene expression data.
DNA Pull-Down assay
The DNA pull-down assay was performed using a DNA pull-down test kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions
[18]
. Briefly, the promoter region of the FOXO1 sequence was amplified by PCR and biotinylated. The biotin-labeled promoters were then incubated with streptavidin-coated magnetic beads (Dynabeads™ M−280 streptavidin; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) at 4 °C for 4 h. A non-biotinylated promoter was used as the negative control, and proteins extracted from primary microglial cells in the input group served as the positive control. The biotinylated promoter-bound beads were incubated with 1 mg of protein extracted from microglial cells with gentle agitation at 4 °C overnight. After incubation, the bead-bound promoter-protein complexes were eluted and analyzed by Western blot for detection of H4K12la.
Pathway inhibition and siRNA transfection
Microglia were plated at a density of 2 × 10
6
cells per well in six-well plates 24 h before transfection. Site-directed mutagenesis was employed to generate the H4-K12R mutants. The cell monolayer reached the desired 70–80 % confluence. Lipo2000 reagent (Invitrogen, USA) was used for plasmid transfection in accordance with the manufacturer's guidelines. For siRNA transfection, cells were transfected at 80 % confluence in 6-well plates with 40 pmol/well of non-targeting control siRNA (con si), P300-targeting siRNA. The media was changed after 2 h. siRNA sequences are listed in
Table S2
.
Cell viability assay
Cell viability was assessed utilizing the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay. Cells were cultured in a 96-well plate and subsequently incubated with the CCK-8 reagent at 37 °C for a duration of 2 h. The optical density (OD) values were measured at a wavelength of 450 nm utilizing a Thermo Multiskan FC microplate photometer.
Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mitoROS) measurement
Microglial cells were cultured in 6-well plates at a density of 6 × 10
4
cells per well. MitoSOX molecular probes (Invitrogen, CA) were employed to detect mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mitoROS) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Post-treatment, the cells were imaged at a wavelength of λ579 nm using a Zeiss Axio Observer 3 microscope.
Assay of malondialdehyde (MDA), glutathione (GSH) and glutathione disulfide (GSSH) concentrations
MDA, GSH, and GSSG levels were assessed with Beyotime Biotech's Lipid Peroxidation MDA Assay Kit (S0131S) and GSH/GSSG Assay Kit (S0053). Following the treatments, the cells were rinsed with PBS at a pH of 7.4, followed by lysis. The lysates were subjected to centrifugation at 12,000 revolutions per minute for a duration of 10 min at a temperature of 4 °C. The absorbance of the supernatant was measured at 532 nm via a microplate reader (Biotech, Winooski, VT, USA). The concentration was normalized to the protein amount of cell lysates.
JC‑1 fuorescence assay
The mitochondrial membrane potential was evaluated through fluorescence imaging of JC-1 (C2003S, Beyotime, China). Microglial cells were incubated with the JC-1 solution for a duration of 20 min at 37 °C, followed by two rinses with JC-1 buffer. Images were captured via a Zeiss Axio Observer 3 microscope. The mitochondrial membrane potential was quantified by the ratio of red to green fluorescence.
Statistical methods
Statistical analyses were performed using two-tailed unpaired Student's t-tests with GraphPad Prism software, unless otherwise indicated. Quantitative data, derived from three independent biological replicates, are presented as means ± standard deviations (SDs). All experiments were conducted with three independent biological replicates unless explicitly stated otherwise. A two-sided p-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Statistical methods
Statistical analyses were performed using two-tailed unpaired Student's t-tests with GraphPad Prism software, unless otherwise indicated. Quantitative data, derived from three independent biological replicates, are presented as means ± standard deviations (SDs). All experiments were conducted with three independent biological replicates unless explicitly stated otherwise. A two-sided p-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Introduction
Diabetes and cognitive impairment are highly prevalent chronic conditions that afflict people globally. Patients with diabetes exhibit a substantially increased risk of progressive cognitive decline, characterized by impairments in memory, cognitive flexibility, and executive function. In severe cases, this can manifest as dementia and behavioral disturbances. Patients with cognitive impairment exhibit a diminished capacity for self-management, resulting in heightened reliance on healthcare professionals. This heightened dependency can serve as a catalyst for the accelerated progression of diabetes. The cognitive deficits that accompany this impairment can impede patients' ability to adhere to treatment regimens, monitor blood glucose levels, and engage in informed decision-making regarding their health. Subsequently, suboptimal glycemic control can precipitate complications and expedite disease progression
[1]
. The prevalence of diabetes-associated cognitive decline (DACD) is substantial, reaching 13.5 % of the population and surpassing 24.2 % among individuals aged 75 and older
[2]
. This significantly increases the economic burden on both families and society at large, constituting a pressing public health concern that demands immediate and comprehensive attention.
The pathogenesis of DACD is intricate. Hyperglycemia induces alterations in neuronal glucose metabolism, resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired cellular energy metabolism, and increased lactate production
[3]
. Lactic acid, a by-product of cellar sugar metabolism, has emerged as a critical molecule in neuronal function. Studies have shown that lactate can function as an alternative energy substrate for neurons, facilitating the protection and regeneration of damaged axons. However, prolonged excessive accumulation of lactate can disrupt intracellular acid-base homeostasis, leading to a state of acidosis. This acidic environment can exacerbate oxidative stress by impairing mitochondrial function and enhancing the reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. Furthermore, lactate-induced acidosis can activate apoptotic pathways, leading to neuronal cell death. Additionally, lactate can modulate various signaling pathways, including those involved in inflammation and neurodegeneration, thereby contributing to the overall impairment of neuronal function
[4]
,
[5]
. As a precursor to protein lactylation (Kla), lactate plays a pivotal role in promoting this post-translational modification
[6]
. Beyond its metabolic function, protein lactylation has been shown to modulate a wide range of cellular processes. These include, but are not limited to, the regulation of glycolysis
[7]
, the polarization of macrophages
[8]
, and the proliferation of tumor cells
[9]
, highlighting its significance in cellular homeostasis. It is ubiquitously expressed across various cell types and has been linked to the development of numerous diseases
[10]
. In neuronal cells, lactate is involved in neuronal regulation through Kla-mediated mechanisms. A recent study demonstrated that exogenous lactate induces a region-specific upregulation of the protein Kla in the brain. The ubiquity of this effect across diverse neuronal cell populations, including astrocytes, microglia, and glutamatergic neurons, highlights its significance in brain function
[11]
. Studies of protein Kla in astrocytes have revealed a robust expression of Kla in astrocytes adjacent to amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques within Alzheimer's disease (AD) mouse models. These findings, coupled with the observation of Kla's association with proinflammatory astrocyte activation, suggest a potential role for Kla in the neuroinflammatory processes underlying AD
[12]
. Kla occurs not only on histones but also on a diverse array of non-histone proteins. Histone lactylation is characterized by the covalent attachment of lactyl groups to lysine residues within histone proteins. This modification alters the electrostatic properties and structural conformation of histones, influencing their interaction with DNA and consequently modulating gene expression. As a critical epigenetic regulator, histone lactylation is implicated in the maintenance of cellular metabolism and normal physiological functions
[13]
. However, the specific role of histone lactylation, particularly in the context of DACD, remains largely unexplored.
In this study, we successfully established a murine model of DACD. Our findings revealed a positive correlation between elevated lactic acid levels and histone lactylation within hippocampal microglia, which was associated with impaired cognitive function. Furthermore, we identified specific histone Kla sites in hippocampal microglia, with a particular emphasis on H4K12la, which was significantly upregulated in DACD mice compared to controls. Employing the CUT&Tag technique, we identified a pronounced enrichment of H4K12la at the promoter regions of FOXO1 pathway-related genes. Notably, lactate dehydrogenase inhibition in high glucose-exposed microglia resulted in a substantial decrease in lactic acid levels, concurrently leading to a marked reduction in H4K12la levels and attenuated FOXO1 pathway activity. These findings collectively demonstrate that elevated H4K12la directly stimulates the FOXO1 signaling pathway, thereby exacerbating mitochondrial oxidative stress and contributing to the development of DACD phenotypes.

Paraffin-embedded tissues were sectioned into 4–5 μm thick slices and mounted onto glass slides. IHC staining was performed using a DAB kit and an IHC kit (ZSGB-BIO, Beijing, China) according to the manufacturer's protocols with anti-4HNE antibody (cat. no. MA5-27570; 1:500 dilution; RRID: AB_2735095, Invitrogen Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China). Following the staining procedure, slides underwent dehydration and clearing processes before being mounted using a permanent mounting medium. Images were captured at a magnification of 400 × utilizing an Olympus BX53 microscope integrated with a digital camera.
TUNEL staining
Apoptosis was evaluated using the TUNEL Apoptosis Assay Kit (C1088, Beyotime, China) in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol. Hippocampal sections were fixed in 4 % paraformaldehyde for a duration of 30 min, followed by two consecutive 10-minute washes in 0.01 M PBS. Permeabilization was achieved through a 5-minute incubation in 0.5 % Triton-X-100/PBS at room temperature. Subsequently, sections were incubated with TUNEL assay solution for 60 min at 37 °C in the dark, protected from evaporation. Nuclear staining was performed using DAPI for 10 min, followed by three 5-minute PBS washes. Coverslips were applied using a 50 % glycerin mounting medium. Stained sections were examined under a fluorescence microscope (Olympus Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) at 200 × magnification. Five randomly selected fields were analyzed to quantify total neurons and TUNEL-positive neurons. The proportion of apoptotic neurons was determined by calculating the ratio of TUNEL-positive neurons to total neurons multiplied by 100 %.
Lactate measurement
After homogenization of frozen hippocampal tissue in 1 mL of ice-cold lactate assay buffer, the samples were centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 5 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was analyzed using an L-lactate assay (cat. no. A019-2–1, Jiancheng, Nanjing, China) to quantify lactate levels following the manufacturer's protocol. For in vitro experiments, cells were harvested by centrifugation, resuspended in pre-cooled PBS, and pelleted again. The supernatant was removed, and the cell pellet was resuspended in 1 mL of lactate assay buffer. Cell disruption was achieved through sonication in an ice bath utilizing a 200 W sonicator. The sonication was performed in 30 cycles, each consisting of a 3-second pulse and a 7-second rest, for a total sonication time of 5 min. Following the initial centrifugation, the resulting supernatant underwent a second centrifugation at 12,000 × g for 5 min at 4 °C. The clarified supernatant was then transferred to a fresh Eppendorf tube. Lactate levels were quantified in both brain tissue homogenates and microglial cell culture supernatants using a commercial lactate analyzer (Roche, Mannheim, Germany).
Quantitative proteomics analysis
Hippocampus samples from each group were measured in triplicate. The proteomic analysis was performed at the Jingjie PTM BioLab Co., Ltd. (Hangzhou, China) Proteomics Facility, following standard protocols. Proteins extracted from hippocampal cell lysates were quantified using the BCA protein assay. For digestion, proteins were subjected to trypsin treatment at a protein-to-protease ratio of 50:1 (w/w) for 12 h. Subsequently, cysteines were reduced and alkylated through sequential incubation with 5 mM dithiothreitol at 56 °C for 30 min, followed by 11 mM iodoacetamide for 15 min at room temperature in the dark. The resulting peptides were resuspended in mobile phase A (0.1 % formic acid + 2 % acetonitrile) for liquid chromatography. Separation was carried out using a NanoElute ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography system (Bruker Daltonics). The gradient for phase B (0.1 % formic acid + 100 % acetonitrile) was as follows: 6–24 % for 0–70 min, 24–35 % for 70–84 min, 35–80 % for 84–87 min, and held at 80 % from 87 to 90 min, with a flow rate of 450 nL/min. During the separation process, peptides were ionized using a capillary ion source and analyzed with a TIMS-TOF Pro mass spectrometer. The pulse voltage was set to 1.65 kV, and both peptide precursors and their secondary fragments were analyzed using high-resolution LC/Q-TOF-MS, with a secondary mass spectrometry scan range of 400 to 1500
m
/
z
.
Differential expression analysis across the three groups was performed using the DESeq2 R software package (version 3.14). Fold-changes were calculated to compare the groups, with proteins showing an adjusted p-value of less than 0.05 and an absolute fold-change greater than 1.2 being considered differentially expressed. Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses for differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were conducted using the clusterProfiler package (version 3.4.4). Cell culture
Primary microglias cultures were derived from C57BL/6 mice in accordance with established protocols. The cortices of two-month-old mice were finely minced in Hibernate A medium supplemented with B27 (Gibco) and subsequently dissociated using a papain solution (Worthington). Following tissue trituration, the cells were isolated via density gradient centrifugation employing Optiprep (Sigma-Aldrich). Primary microgliass were maintained in either high- or low-glucose Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS, GibcoBRL) at 37 °C with 5 % CO2. Human monocytic cell line HMC3 (RRID: CVCL_II76) was cultured in Minimum Essential Medium (MEM) supplemented with Non-Essential Amino Acids (NEAA) and 10 % FBS. Cells were subcultured every 3 to 4 days and maintained in a temperature-controlled incubator set at 37 °C. Microglials were cultured at a density of 1 × 10
6
cells per well in a six-well plate. Cells were cultured with or without NaLa (25 μM, Sigma-Aldrich, MO, USA) and incubated for 24 h. In order to investigate the mechanisms underlying diabetes, we modeled the in vivo diabetic state using a well-established in vitro system of HG and Pal
[17]
. Cells were treated with an HG + Pal medium, consisting of 200 μM palmitate and 25 mM glucose. To assess the role of LDH, we inhibited its activity by treating cells with 50 mM oxamate for 2 h prior to subsequent experiments.
Western blot analysis
Total protein concentration in both in vitro and in vivo microglia was quantified prior to sample preparation. Subsequently, a loading buffer was added to the protein samples, which were then subjected to denaturation through high-temperature incubation. Following denaturation, protein samples were resolved by SDS-PAGE (Wako Supersep™Ace, 5–20 %) and subsequently transferred to PVDF membranes (Invitrogen) using transfer buffer. To minimize non-specific binding, membranes were blocked using a 5 % solution of non-fat blocking grade milk. Primary antibodies against Pan Kla (RRID:AB_2942013, Jingjie PTM BioLabs, Hangzhou, China), histone H3K18 (RRID:AB_3076698, Jingjie PTM BioLabs, Hangzhou, China), histone H4K12 (RRID:AB_2941896, Jingjie PTM BioLabs, Hangzhou, China), histone H4K8 (RRID: AB_3101829, Jingjie PTM BioLabs, Hangzhou, China), histone H4 (RRID: AB_3101866, Jingjie PTM BioLabs, Hangzhou, China), CBP (cat. no. 7389; RRID: AB_2616020, Cell Signaling Technology, Massachusetts, USA), P300 (cat. no. 57625; RRID: AB_3068009, Cell Signaling Technology, Massachusetts, USA), FOXO1 (cat. no. MA5-14846; RRID: AB_10987316, Invitrogen Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China) and PGC-1α (cat. no. ab191838; RRID: AB_2721267, Abcam, Cambridge, UK) were applied to the blots overnight. After incubation with TBST, protein bands were probed with a secondary antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Boston, MA, USA) for 1 h at room temperature. ECL was employed to visualize the immunoreactive bands. Densitometric analysis was conducted using ImageJ software to quantify the specific antibody fluorescence intensity of the protein bands.
Immunofuorescent staining
Following deparaffinization and rehydration, sections were subjected to antigen retrieval. Nonspecific binding was blocked by incubating sections with goat serum for 1 h at room temperature. Subsequently, sections were incubated with primary antibodies against Iba1 (cat. no. MA5-50414; 1:500 dilution; RRID: AB_3094208, Invitrogen Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China), Pan Kla (cat. no. PTM-1401RM; 1:100 dilution; RRID:AB_2942013, PTM BIO, Hangzhou, China), H4K12la (cat. no. PTM-1415RM; 1:100 dilution; RRID:AB_2941896, PTM BIO, Hangzhou, China), Aβ (cat. no. MA1-140; 1:500 dilution; RRID: AB_2536844, Invitrogen Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China), FOXO1 (cat. no. MA5-14846; 1:500 dilution; RRID: AB_10987316, Invitrogen Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China), incubated with secondary antibodies conjugated with Alexa Fluor dyes: Alexa Fluor 488 (green), Alexa Fluor 594 (red), and Alexa Fluor 750 (pink) (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China), and then mounted on slides. Immunofluorescence-stained sections were visualized and captured at high resolution with a Zeiss Axio Observer 3 fluorescence microscope. ImageJ software was utilized to measure the mean fluorescence intensity within defined regions of interest. Iba1- and Kla-positive cells were manually counted to determine cell numbers.
Human specimens
We recruited 42 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and 35 healthy controls from individuals undergoing physical examinations at Tangshan Gongren Hospital. Participants were recruited between January 2022 and May 2022. The diagnostic criteria for T2DM were based on the World Health Organization's recommendations. Clinical information was gathered from medical records. Global cognitive function was assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Fasting blood samples were drawn from the cubital vein with the subject supine. Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of Tangshan Gongren Hospital.
Metabolomic analysis
Metabolomics analysis was conducted using UPLC-Q-TOF/MS. After pre-processing, the analysis was performed on an ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography system (UHPLC, 1290 Infinity LC, Agilent Technologies) coupled with a quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometer (AB Sciex TripleTOF 6600) at Shanghai Applied Protein Technology Co., Ltd. For HILIC separation, a 2.1 mm × 100 mm ACQUIY UPLC BEH column (1.7 µm, Waters, Ireland) was used. The raw mass spectrometry (MS) data were converted to MzXML format using ProteoWizard MSConvert and subsequently processed with the open-source software XCMS. For peak detection, the following parameters were applied: centWave

= 10 ppm, peakwidth = c(10, 60), and prefilter = c(10, 100). For peak grouping, the settings were bw = 5, mzwid = 0.025, and minfrac = 0.5. Isotope and adduct annotation were carried out using the CAMERA (Collection of Algorithms of MEtabolite pRofile Annotation) package. From the extracted ion features, only variables with more than 50 % non-zero measurement values in at least one group were retained. Metabolite identification was performed by comparing the accurate
m
/

values (<10 ppm) and MS/MS spectra against an in-house database established using authentic standards.
Isolation of microglia from adult mouse brains
Following euthanasia by intraperitoneal pentobarbital injection, mice subjected to transcardial perfusion using ice-cold phosphate-buffered saline. Brains were carefully extracted and placed on a chilled dissection plate. The cortex, olfactory bulbs, and cerebellum were removed, and the bilateral hippocampi were bilaterally dissected and collected. Tissue dissociation was was conducted using the Adult Brain Dissociation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, Germany), strictly adhering to the manufacturer's guidelines. Following myelin removal using cell debris removal buffers, the total cell pellet was resuspended in PBS supplemented with 0.5 % BSA to facilitate the subsequent isolation of specific cell types. Microglia were isolated by positive selection utilizing anti-CD11b-coated MicroBeads (130–093-634, Miltenyi Biotec) and a MACS multistand separator, as per the manufacturer’s protocol. For histone extraction and analysis, cells from three mice were pooled for each experimental sample. After confirmation by immunofluorescence, the sorted cells did not exhibit polarization and showed either no or very few cellular protrusions (
Fig. S1
).
CUT&Tag and sequencing
Isolated microglia were subjected to CUT&Tag analysis immediately following isolation. The CUT&Tag protocol was carried out according to the manufacturer's instructions using the Hieff NGS® G-Type In- situ DNA Binding Profiling Library Prep Kit for Illumina (12598ES12, Yeasen, Shanghai, China). Isolated microglia were bound to Concanavalin A-coated beads and subsequently resuspended in antibody buffer for incubation with primary antibodies specific for H4K12la. Following this, cells were incubated with corresponding secondary antibodies. Transposon activation and tagmentation of the samples were achieved using pA-Tn5 transposase. The resulting DNA fragments were subsequently isolated, amplified, and purified to generate sequencing libraries. High-throughput sequencing was conducted on an Illumina NovaSeq system, employing paired-end 150-base reads.
Real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR)
Total RNA was isolated from tissues or cells using a Trizol-based cell lysis buffer (Invitrogen, CA, USA). cDNA was subsequently synthesized from the extracted RNA using a PrimeScript™ RT reagent kit (cat. no. RR037A; Takara Bio, Inc., Dalian, China). Quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) was performed using SYBR-Green mix (Roche, Basel, Switzerland) to determine gene expression levels. Primer sequences utilized for qPCR are provided in
Table S1
. β-actin mRNA levels served as an endogenous control for normalization of gene expression data.
DNA Pull-Down assay
The DNA pull-down assay was performed using a DNA pull-down test kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions
[18]
. Briefly, the promoter region of the FOXO1 sequence was amplified by PCR and biotinylated. The biotin-labeled promoters were then incubated with streptavidin-coated magnetic beads (Dynabeads™ M−280 streptavidin; Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) at 4 °C for 4 h. A non-biotinylated promoter was used as the negative control, and proteins extracted from primary microglial cells in the input group served as the positive control. The biotinylated promoter-bound beads were incubated with 1 mg of protein extracted from microglial cells with gentle agitation at 4 °C overnight. After incubation, the bead-bound promoter-protein complexes were eluted and analyzed by Western blot for detection of H4K12la.
Pathway inhibition and siRNA transfection
Microglia were plated at a density of 2 × 10
6
cells per well in six-well plates 24 h before transfection. Site-directed mutagenesis was employed to generate the H4-K12R mutants. The cell monolayer reached the desired 70–80 % confluence. Lipo2000 reagent (Invitrogen, USA) was used for plasmid transfection in accordance with the manufacturer's guidelines. For siRNA transfection, cells were transfected at 80 % confluence in 6-well plates with 40 pmol/well of non-targeting control siRNA (con si), P300-targeting siRNA. The media was changed after 2 h. siRNA sequences are listed in
Table S2
.
Cell viability assay
Cell viability was assessed utilizing the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay. Cells were cultured in a 96-well plate and subsequently incubated with the CCK-8 reagent at 37 °C for a duration of 2 h. The optical density (OD) values were measured at a wavelength of 450 nm utilizing a Thermo Multiskan FC microplate photometer.
Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mitoROS) measurement
Microglial cells were cultured in 6-well plates at a density of 6 × 10
4
cells per well. MitoSOX molecular probes (Invitrogen, CA) were employed to detect mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mitoROS) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions. Post-treatment, the cells were imaged at a wavelength of λ579 nm using a Zeiss Axio Observer 3 microscope.
Assay of malondialdehyde (MDA), glutathione (GSH) and glutathione disulfide (GSSH) concentrations
MDA, GSH, and GSSG levels were assessed with Beyotime Biotech's Lipid Peroxidation MDA Assay Kit (S0131S) and GSH/GSSG Assay Kit (S0053). Following the treatments, the cells were rinsed with PBS at a pH of 7.4, followed by lysis. The lysates were subjected to centrifugation at 12,000 revolutions per minute for a duration of 10 min at a temperature of 4 °C. The absorbance of the supernatant was measured at 532 nm via a microplate reader (Biotech, Winooski, VT, USA). The concentration was normalized to the protein amount of cell lysates.
JC‑1 fuorescence assay
The mitochondrial membrane potential was evaluated through fluorescence imaging of JC-1 (C2003S, Beyotime, China). Microglial cells were incubated with the JC-1 solution for a duration of 20 min at 37 °C, followed by two rinses with JC-1 buffer. Images were captured via a Zeiss Axio Observer 3 microscope. The mitochondrial membrane potential was quantified by the ratio of red to green fluorescence.
Statistical methods
Statistical analyses were performed using two-tailed unpaired Student's t-tests with GraphPad Prism software, unless otherwise indicated. Quantitative data, derived from three independent biological replicates, are presented as means ± standard deviations (SDs). All experiments were conducted with three independent biological replicates unless explicitly stated otherwise. A two-sided p-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Hyperglycaemia can cause pathological damage in hippocampal and neuronal apoptosis
Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated a marked increase in 4HNE immunoreactivity within hippocampal neurons of T2DM mice compared to control animals (
Fig. 2
A). These findings suggest an upregulation of oxidative stress in the hippocampus of diabetic mice. Neuronal morphology and abundance in the hippocampus of control mice were examined using H&E staining. The hippocampal neurons in the control group demonstrated a normal, well-preserved morphology, characterized by distinct cellular boundaries and nuclear structures (
Fig. 2
B). Hyperglycemia in T2DM mice led to a marked decrease in neuronal count and structural integrity within the hippocampus and cortex. Microscopic evaluation revealed pronounced cellular damage and pyknotic nuclei in T2DM mice. Importantly, the hippocampus is recognized as a critical component in cognitive function, and its dysfunction is a hallmark of cognitive decline in T2DM patients. The increased number of TUNEL-positive cells observed in the hippocampus of T2DM mice, as compared to controls (
Fig. 2
C), provides evidence that hyperglycemia may induce hippocampal damage and promote neuronal apoptosis.

Discussion
Diabetes is frequently accompanied by cognitive decline, a common complication and comorbidity of the disease
[20]
,
[21]
. Diabetes mellitus, particularly type 2 diabetes, has traditionally been associated with older age groups. However, in recent decades, a notable increase in the incidence of diabetes has been observed among younger adults and even adolescents
[22]
. While DACD can manifest across all age groups, the prevalence of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia exhibits a marked increase with age. These conditions are relatively uncommon in individuals under 65 years, including those with diabetes, but their incidence doubles every five years post-65
[23]
. T2DM has been associated with a subtle yet pervasive cognitive impairment across all age groups. Manifestations include deficits in memory, processing speed, and executive functioning, often progressing gradually over time. Individuals with T2DM exhibit an elevated relative risk for developing mild cognitive impairment and dementia
[24]
. Despite extensive research, the progression and pathogenesis of this disease is intricate, multifactorial, and not yet fully comprehended.
[25]
,
[26]
. DACD represents a culmination of the long-term detrimental effects of DM on the brain, primarily attributed to disruptions in energy metabolism
[1]
,
[27]
,
[28]
. Recent studies have demonstrated that lactate, a metabolic byproduct traditionally viewed as a waste product, can directly modulate gene transcription. By covalently modifying histones through lactylation, lactate has emerged as a novel epigenetic regulator, responding dynamically to changes in cellular metabolic state
[29]
,
[30]
,
[31]
. The present study elucidates lactate as a key signaling molecule involved in regulating post-translational modifications and influencing the epigenetic landscape
[32]
. Simlar to other histone acylation modifications, histone lactylation has been experimentally shown to directly promote gene transcription by altering chromatin structure and facilitating the recruitment of transcriptional machinery. Emerging evidence underscores the significance of histone lactylation in regulating a broad spectrum of biological processes. Studies have highlighted its crucial role in macrophage M1 polarization and cellular senescence. Furthermore, a growing body of literature links aberrant histone lactylation to the pathogenesis of various diseases, such as AD
[33]
,
[34]
. Investigations into high-glucose and medium-glucose cohorts, coupled with hyperglycemic animal models, have revealed a strong correlations between elevated cerebral l-lactate levels and the pathophysiology of diabetes and AD. Furthermore, our study reveals that elevated lactate levels in the hippocampal region are associated with a marked impairment in cognitive performance, suggesting that excessive lactate secretion may play a causal role in cognitive dysfunction
[28]
,
[35]
,
[36]
. Our study revealed a strong association between T2DM and cognitive dysfunction. As the disease advanced, T2DM mice exhibited significant deficits in memory and learning tasks. Our findings demonstrated a pronounced elevation in hippocampal and cortical lactate concentrations in DACD mice, indicative of a metabolic transition from OXPHOS to aerobic glycolysis. This shift facilitated rapid 5′-triphosphate (ATP) synthesis but concomitantly resulted in substantial lactate accumulation. Ma et al.
[37]
applied single cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) to capture T2DM-induced gene changes in hippocampal cells and found that microglia play an important role in the cellular functional network. Lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) was upregulated in hippocampal microglia of diabetic mice, indicating that lactate metabolism may undergo changes in microglia under diabetic conditions. Additionally, the hyperglycemic condition promoted lactate accumulation, which subsequently upregulated histone Kla expression, thus exacerbating cognitive dysfunction and amyloid-beta plaque formation. Furthermore, the hyperglycemic state induced lactate accumulation, leading to an upregulation of histone Kla expression. Consequently, this molecular cascade exacerbated cognitive dysfunction and amyloid-beta plaque formation.
Protein lactylation, a post-translational modification, is characterized by the covalent attachment of a lactate group to lysine residues. This modification can occur on both histones and non-histone proteins. While both types of lactylation have been observed, histone lactylation has emerged as a critical regulator of gene expression
[38]
. Histones, nuclear proteins found exclusively in eukaryotic cells, are essential for the organization and compaction of DNA into chromatin
[39]
,
[40]
,
[41]
. The core function of histones is to package DNA into discrete structural units known as nucleosomes. These nucleosomes constitute the foundational building blocks of chromatin, facilitating the efficient compaction of the genome within the nucleus
[42]
,
[43]
. Histones are fundamental proteins that are characterized by their small size and a high proportion of positively charged amino acids, which facilitate their strong binding to the negatively charged phosphate backbone of DNA. Five primary histone proteins have been identified: H1, H2A, H2B, H3, and H4
[44]
. The nucleosome core particle is constituted by an octameric assembly of histone proteins, comprising two molecules each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. This histone octamer is encircled by approximately 147 base pairs of DNA
[45]
,
[46]
. Such packaging facilitates the dense packing of DNA, regulating the accessibility of genetic material and impacting essential biological processes like gene expression, DNA replication, and repair
[47]
. We observed a striking group difference in H4K12 lactylation specifically within microglia of T2DM mice. Given the established significance of H4K12 lactylation in a diverse array of pathologies, including cancer, atherosclerosis, and neurodegenerative diseases, our results highlight a novel avenue for investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying T2DM
[12]
,
[47]
,
[48]
. Lactation of lysine 12 on histone H4, characterized by the covalent attachment of lactyl groups to this specific residue within the flexible H4 histone tail, represents a prevalent post-translational modification. This modification exerts a regulatory influence on chromatin architecture and gene transcription, thereby impacting cellular processes and disease states. Through bioinformatics analysis, we discovered several upstream regulatory factors of H4K12la (
Fig. S8
). Aberrant H4K12 lactylation patterns have been associated with dysregulated transcriptional programs, compromised DNA repair pathways, and perturbed signaling cascades, collectively contributing to the pathogenesis of various diseases
[33]
. A comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms driving H4K12 lactylation in diverse disease states may pave the way for the design of novel therapeutic approaches.
We also identified the acetyltransferase p300/CBP as a histone lactylase (a “writer”) in both primary microglia and HMC3 cells, partially confirming the earlier findings of Zhang et al.
[31]
and Wei et al.
[32]
. Our CUT&Tag analysis of the epigenetic mechanism, along with verification experiments, revealed that H4K12la activates the FOXO1/PGC-1α pathway, promoting mitochondrial oxidative stress. Intracerebroventricular injection of AAV-HDAC3-EYFP enhances de-S-acylation by increasing HDAC3 activity. This suppresses histone lactylation, thereby inhibiting the FOXO1/PGC-1α pathway. Downregulation of histone H4 lactylation at K12 reduces the FOXO1 pathway, oxidative stress levels, and cell apoptosis. These findings indicate that the metabolic shift to aerobic glycolysis in HG-induced microglia worsens DACD by targeting oxidative stress through the H4K12la/FOXO1 signaling axis. Our findings expand the understanding of the biological roles of histone Kla and its regulated downstream targets. Preliminary results indicate that the H4K12la/FOXO1/PGC-1α signaling axis in HG-treated microglia can exacerbate the DACD phenotype by enhancing neuro-oxidative stress. Together, these findings indicate that histone lactylation influences various molecular mechanisms by targeting specific genes and pathways in microglia, ultimately leading to neuronal damage and cognitive decline. Our validation experiments revealed that elevated levels of H4K12la enhance binding to the FOXO1 promoter, which amplifies downstream signaling and promotes mitochondrial oxidation, significantly affecting mitochondrial function. Our research suggests that the H4K12la/FOXO1/mitochondrial oxidation axis is crucial in driving the pathogenesis of DACD.
Regarding whether the onset of DACD or other neurological disorders is related to the crosstalk between H4K12la and other epigenetic modifications, some research teams have published findings. Firstly, H4K12la may exhibit crosstalk with histone acetylation, such as H4K12ac. Both H4K12la and H4K12ac modify the same lysine residue on histone H4, potentially competing with or influencing each other's presence. This competition can impact chromatin structure and gene transcription. Research has shown that in conditions like AD, metabolic changes can alter the balance between lactylation and acetylation, which in turn affects genes involved in neuroinflammation and synaptic function
[33]
. Secondly, histone lactylation may influence histone methylation patterns by altering chromatin accessibility or affecting the recruitment of methyltransferases and demethylases. Disruptions in the interactions between lactylation and methylation could interfere with gene expression profiles linked to neurodegenerative diseases, potentially impacting neuronal function and survival
[49]
. The crosstalk between H4K12la and other epigenetic modifications plays a significant role in regulating gene expression in the CNS Whether this crosstalk contributes to the regulation of DACD gene expression requires further experimental investigation. It is essential to acknowledge several limitations of the current study. The inability to generate animal models with site-specific histone H4 mutations prevented a direct assessment of the effects of these mutations on FOXO1 and mitochondrial oxidative stress in vivo. Future investigations will focus on identifying the precise lactylases and delactylases, as well as the associated proteins that install, remove, and/or recognize H4K12la. In future research, we will also focus on addressing issues such as additional intervention strategies and sex differences in therapeutic responses. Furthermore, future experimental approaches should incorporate technologies such as single-cell spatial transcriptomics, which can map gene expression patterns within the context of tissue architecture, providing deeper insights into the molecular mechanisms involved. A more comprehensive understanding of these molecular mechanisms will elucidate the role of this modification in regulating microglial function in the context of T2DM.
In summary, these findings reveal a novel molecular pathway where the H4K12la/FOXO1 axis coordinates neurological function by regulating mitochondrial oxidative stress and cell survival, contributing to the development of DACD phenotypes (
Fig. 8
). These insights highlight potential targets for developing drug interventions to address DACD pathology.
